The Western jackdaw (Coloeus monedula) typically weighs around 260 grams [Wwi = around 260 grams] upon reaching full adulthood, a body mass that positions it among the smaller members of the Corvidae family. Neonates, in contrast, emerge from the egg at a substantially lower mass of approximately 11.3 grams [Wwb = approximately 11.3 grams], reflecting the altricial developmental strategy characteristic of most corvids. This steep increase in body mass—from hatchling to adult—is supported by intensive biparental provisioning throughout the nestling period. Hatchlings are entirely dependent on their parents for warmth and food, and their rapid growth trajectory is fueled by a diet rich in invertebrates. The metabolic machinery required to sustain such development can be appreciated through respirometric measurements taken under controlled conditions. Specifically, the basal metabolic rate of adult jackdaws reaches its maximum at a value of 309.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 309.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a rate that underscores the energetic demands of homeothermy in a bird of this size.

The tight thermal regulation provided by the incubating adult is critical; deviations from this optimal temperature can prolong embryonic development or reduce hatch success. Once hatched, the altricial nestlings undergo a period of rapid feather growth and mass accumulation within the nest cavity. The timeline to fledging, marking the point at which a young bird achieves its first sustained flight, is reached at 35 days after hatching [tx = 35 days after hatching] under typical brooding temperatures of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This developmental milestone is a critical transition, as the fledgling must then navigate the challenges of learning to forage while still relying partially on parental food deliveries.

Most pairs successfully fledge a single brood each year [F_R_i = single brood each year], though replacement clutches may be attempted if the first is lost early in incubation. The intervening years are spent in juvenile and sub-adult flocks, where young birds practice pair-bonding behaviors and learn the intricacies of territory defense and nest construction. The extended pre-breeding period is thought to be a key life-history adaptation that reduces the risk of reproductive failure among inexperienced individuals.
